mainTopic: A גט over two columns, where witnesses must sign, the scribe as witness, ancestral nicknames, and aggadot on why ישראל went into exile
overview: The amud finishes a discussion of a גט written over two columns. Blank space above the second column, or the sentence "הרי את / מותרת" running across the break, shows it is one continuous גט. רב אשי gives a different answer: the sheet itself shows it was never cut. Next, the גמרא asks how רב could sign on the side when the משנה says such a גט is invalid. After one answer is knocked down, it concludes that רב signed only letters that way. רבי ירמיה then teaches that a scribe counts as a witness only if he signed, and he applies this to a real כתובה brought before רבי אבהו. The גמרא discusses how many generations an ancestral nickname stays valid in a גט, and רב הונא learns three generations from 'ונושנתם'. This leads into aggadic teachings: the land was destroyed only after seven idol-worshipping royal houses, and the exile came in הושע בן אלה's days because the people chose not to go up for the רגל. Finally, two answers explain how God's bringing the exile was צדקה: the scholars were already waiting in בבל, or the exile came two years early so the threat of total destruction never came true.

steps.title: Blank space above the second column shows it continues
steps.stepSummary: The case is one where there is empty space above the second column, so it is clearly part of the same document.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here too, it is a case where there is space above.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes an answer it began earlier. Just as in the other case, here too there is empty space at the top of the second column.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry was that the two columns might really be two separate documents. Blank space at the top of the second column shows that this column is not a new, separate document. It simply continues the first column.

keyTerms.meaning: here too, in the same way

phrases.english: So too here,
it is where there is space above.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the answer begun just before this part of the daf.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defines the case narrowly (there is space above the second column).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two columns might be two separate גיטין.
steps.terutzMaskana: Space above the second column shows it is one continuous גט.

steps.title: Maybe the husband changed his mind partway through
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: even if it is one document, maybe the husband stopped and cancelled partway, then later had the rest written.
steps.simpleTranslation: But perhaps he changed his mind, and then wrote the rest!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a new worry. Even if this is one document, maybe the writing of the גט was interrupted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Showing that it is one document does not show that it was written in one go. If the husband changed his mind after the first column, the first part would be cancelled. Then the second column would have been added to a dead document.

phrases.english: But perhaps he changed his mind
(and wrote)!
phrases.notes: These words are in round brackets: the standard printed text has them, but some versions leave them out.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts that it is one document but attacks whether it was written in one go.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer in step 1 that space above proves one valid גט.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: One document can still have been written in two stages, with the husband changing his mind in between.

steps.title: The sentence runs straight across the two columns
steps.stepSummary: The case is one where "הרי את" ends the first column and "מותרת" begins the second.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is where he wrote "You are hereby" at the bottom of the first column, and "permitted" at the top of the second.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that a single sentence is split across the two columns.
steps.deeperAnalysis: "הרי את מותרת לכל אדם" is the key sentence of the גט. If the break falls in the middle of that sentence, it looks like he just kept writing without stopping.

phrases.english: Where he wrote "You are hereby" at the bottom,
phrases.notes: He means at the bottom of the first column.

phrases.english: and "permitted" at the top.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the worry of step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrows the case so the writing is clearly continuous.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: He may have stopped and changed his mind between the columns.
steps.terutzMaskana: A sentence split mid-phrase shows he wrote straight through.

steps.title: Maybe he happened to stop right in the middle
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: perhaps it just happened that he stopped and changed his mind right in the middle of the sentence.
steps.simpleTranslation: But perhaps it just happened to him that way?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on step 3. Maybe the break in the middle of the sentence was just a coincidence.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer in step 3 assumes nobody stops in the middle of a sentence. The challenge says it is still possible that he did.

keyTerms.meaning: it happened to him by chance

phrases.english: But perhaps it just happened to him?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 3 that a split sentence proves continuous writing.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A stop in the middle of the sentence is unlikely, but it is still possible.

steps.title: We don't worry about something so unlikely
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that we are not concerned about such a far-fetched possibility.
steps.simpleTranslation: We are not concerned to such an extent.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא dismisses the worry because it is too unlikely to take seriously.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Halacha does not chase every remote possibility. Stopping and changing his mind exactly in the middle of "הרי את מותרת" is too unlikely to make the גט invalid.
steps.whatToRemember: A גט written over two columns is valid when the second column has space above it and one sentence ("הרי את / מותרת") runs across the break. We ignore the far-fetched idea that he stopped exactly there.

phrases.english: We are not concerned to such an extent.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the worry raised in step 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Dismisses the worry as too unlikely.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: He may have stopped exactly mid-sentence.
steps.terutzMaskana: So remote a possibility is ignored.

steps.title: רב אשי: the sheet itself shows nothing was cut
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי gives a different answer: the case is one where it is clear from the sheet that it is one whole piece of parchment.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: it is a case where the lower part of the scroll is recognizable.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי answers the original worry differently. We can tell from the parchment itself that it is one whole, uncut sheet.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier answer relied on blank space above the second column. רב אשי instead relies on how the sheet looks: it is plainly one piece, so this cannot be two separate גיטין.

keyTerms.meaning: an אמורא who gives his own answer here
where it is recognizable or clear in it
the scroll or sheet of parchment

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
Where the stretch of the scroll is clear in it.
phrases.notes: Literally "the lower part of the scroll is recognizable." He means you can see it is one whole sheet that was never cut.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different answer instead of the one in step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A different way of defining the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The columns might be separate גיטין.
steps.terutzMaskana: The parchment visibly shows it is one uncut sheet.

steps.title: Quoting the משנה about witnesses signing at the top of the sheet
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's ruling that if the עדים signed at the top or side of the sheet, the גט is invalid.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: if the witnesses signed at the top of the sheet (or on the side), the גט is invalid.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a new line of the משנה to start a new discussion. This is a setup line for the question that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה's rule is that the signatures of the עדים must come after the writing of the גט. If they are at the top or off to the side, they are not attached to the text in the normal way, so the גט is not valid.

keyTerms.meaning: Etc.: the quote continues in the משנה

phrases.english: The witnesses signed at the top of the column, etc.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, moving on from the earlier discussion about whether the גט is one sheet.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A גט whose עדים signed at the top or side of the sheet is invalid.

steps.title: But רב used to sign on the side
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the משנה: רב himself would sign on the side of documents.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that really so? Didn't רב sign on the side?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how signing on the side can be invalid when the great אמורא רב used to sign that way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge uses how רב actually behaved. If signing on the side ruins a document, רב would never have done it, so the משנה's rule seems too broad.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that so? (an expression of surprise)

phrases.english: Is that so?!
But Rav would sign on the side!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִינִי? וְהָא רַב חָתֵים מִן הַצַּד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the משנה's rule quoted in step 7.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's rule that signing on the side is invalid.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב signed on the side, so it cannot be invalid in every case.

steps.title: רב turned the top of his signature toward the text
steps.stepSummary: רב's side signature had its top facing the writing, so it clearly belonged to that document.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, רב signed so that the top of his letters faced the text of the document.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רב's way of signing on the side was special: the top of his signature pointed at the writing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The main question is whether the signature is clearly connected to the text. When the top of the signature faces the writing, everyone can see it belongs to that document. The משנה's invalid side signature is one without that clear connection.

keyTerms.meaning: Roof: here, the top of the letters

phrases.english: There, it was with its roof facing the text.
phrases.notes: "Roof" means the top of the letters of his signature, which pointed toward the writing of the document.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from רב in step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the case: רב's signature was turned toward the text.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any signature on the side is invalid, so רב's practice contradicts the משנה.
steps.terutzMaskana: A side signature is fine if its top faces the text. The משנה means one that does not.

steps.title: Then why not check which bill the signatures face?
steps.stepSummary: The משנה invalidates two גיטין written head-to-head with the signatures between them. By the last answer, we should just see which גט the signatures face.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the משנה teaches: if he wrote two גיטין top-to-top with the witnesses in the middle, both are invalid. Why not see which גט the signatures face, and make that one valid?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא uses its last answer to raise a problem with another case in the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 9 said that a signature's direction shows which text it belongs to. In the head-to-head case, the signatures must face one of the two גיטין, so that one should be valid. Yet the משנה says both are invalid.

phrases.english: But that which is taught:
If he placed the top of this bill
next to the top of that bill,
phrases.notes: Two גיטין on one sheet, written in opposite directions, so their tops meet in the middle.

phrases.english: and the witnesses signed in the middle –
both are invalid;
let us see which of them the signatures face,
and let it be valid!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the idea in step 9 that a signature's direction ties it to a text.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer in step 9, that direction determines which text a signature belongs to.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If direction decides, one of the two head-to-head גיטין should be valid, yet the משנה says both are invalid.

steps.title: The signatures were written crosswise, like a bolt
steps.stepSummary: In the head-to-head case, the signatures ran crosswise to both texts, so they faced neither גט.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, the signatures were placed like a door bolt, crosswise to the writing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that in that case the signatures ran sideways, so they did not face either גט.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the signatures run across the lines of both texts, there is no direction to show which גט they belong to. That is why both are invalid, and step 9's rule still stands.

phrases.english: There, it is where they are placed like a bolt.
phrases.notes: Like a bolt across a door: the signatures run sideways, at a right angle to the lines of both גיטין.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 10 by limiting the משנה's case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case: the signatures face neither text.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The signatures must face one of the גיטין, so one should be valid.
steps.terutzMaskana: The signatures run crosswise, so they belong to neither גט, and both are invalid.

steps.title: The next clause shows the signatures belong to one bill
steps.stepSummary: The סיפא validates the גט whose end the signatures follow. That would be impossible if the signatures ran crosswise.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, look at the next clause: top of one next to the end of the other, witnesses in the middle. The one the witnesses are read at the end of is valid. But if the signatures run crosswise, they are not read with either one!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the bolt answer from the next clause of the same משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The סיפא uses the same layout of two גיטין with signatures between them, and it says one גט is valid. That only works if the signatures read together with that גט. If the רישא was talking about crosswise signatures, the סיפא would be too, and then neither גט could be valid.

keyTerms.meaning: The latter clause of the משנה

steps.confusionAlert: The challenge depends on the רישא and סיפא describing the same style of signing. The only difference between them is how the two גיטין are lined up.

phrases.english: If so, the latter clause which teaches:

phrases.aramaic: רֹאשׁוֹ שֶׁל זֶה בְּצַד סוֹפוֹ שֶׁל זֶה,
phrases.english: the top of this bill next to the end of that bill,
and the witnesses in the middle –
the one at whose end the witnesses are read is valid.
And if they are placed like a bolt –
they are not read with this one,
and they are not read with that one!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the bolt answer of step 11 from the next clause of the same משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer in step 11 that the משנה's signatures run crosswise like a bolt.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The סיפא calls one גט valid because the signatures read with it. Crosswise signatures read with neither, so the bolt answer cannot fit the משנה.

steps.title: רב only signed letters on the side
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא drops its earlier answer. רב's side signatures were only on letters, not on legal documents.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב would sign letters that way.
steps.whatsHappening: The last answer, about which way the signatures face, just fell apart. So the גמרא gives a brand-new answer: רב only signed letters on the side, never גיטין or money documents.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The קשיא from step 8 was: how could רב sign on the side if the משנה invalidates side signatures? Now the answer is that the משנה's rule is for legal documents like a גט, which must be signed below the text. A letter is not a legal document, so where the signature goes doesn't matter.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather. It signals that the earlier answer is being dropped.
Letters or written messages, not formal legal documents

steps.whatToRemember: The rule that signatures must sit under the text applies to legal documents like a גט. Letters don't follow that rule, which explains what רב did.

phrases.english: Rather, Rav would sign letters [on the side].

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא from step 8 in a new way, after step 12 knocked down the answer from step 9.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case: רב's practice was only with non-legal writings.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought רב signed legal documents on the side, with his signature facing the text.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב signed only letters on the side. Legal documents must still be signed beneath the text.

steps.title: Quoting the משנה: a scribe's writing plus one witness
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a new line from the משנה: a גט with the scribe's writing and one witness is valid.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'A גט written in Hebrew, etc.,' and 'the writing of a scribe and one witness is valid.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is starting a new topic by quoting a line from the משנה. This sets up the next step, where רבי ירמיה explains what this line really means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a גט needs two witnesses. Read simply, the משנה seems to say the scribe's handwriting can count as one of them, together with one real witness. The next step will question that simple reading.

keyTerms.meaning: The scribe who writes the document

phrases.english: A bill of divorce that was written in Hebrew, etc.
The writing of a scribe and a witness: valid.

steps.triggerLanguage: גֵּט שֶׁכְּתָבוֹ עִבְרִית וְכוּ׳ כָּתַב סוֹפֵר וְעֵד כָּשֵׁר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new section of the משנה, separate from the signature-placement discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A גט with a scribe's writing and one witness is valid.

steps.title: רבי ירמיה: the scribe must have signed
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה says the correct wording is 'the scribe signed,' not 'the scribe wrote.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה said: We learned 'the scribe signed.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ירמיה corrects how we read the משנה. It doesn't mean the scribe's handwriting in the text counts. It means the scribe signed his name as a witness.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just writing the text of the גט is not testimony. Only signing counts as a witness. So the 'two witnesses' are the scribe, who signed, and one more witness.

keyTerms.meaning: We learned (this is the correct wording of the משנה)

steps.confusionAlert: Watch the two look-alike words: כָּתַב means 'wrote' and חָתַם means 'signed.' רבי ירמיה is saying the right word here is חָתַם.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya said:
We learned: 'the scribe signed.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה חָתַם סוֹפֵר שָׁנִינוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the wording of the משנה line quoted in step 14.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The scribe counts as a witness only if he signed. His handwriting in the text is not enough.

steps.title: רב חסדא: the משנה follows רבי יוסי
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא says which תנא this משנה matches: רבי יוסי.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said: Whose view is this? It is רבי יוסי.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא tells us which תנא's opinion this ruling follows. He says it matches רבי יוסי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Accepting a scribe who signed as one of the witnesses fits רבי יוסי's view. On that view, there is no worry that the scribe signed improperly. Naming the תנא shows this is not everyone's opinion.

keyTerms.meaning: The תנא whose view this משנה follows

phrases.english: Rav Chisda said:
Whose is this? It is Rabbi Yosei.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא הָא מַנִּי רַבִּי יוֹסֵי הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Names the תנא behind the ruling that step 15 just explained.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The ruling that a scribe and one witness make a valid גט follows רבי יוסי.

steps.title: A כתובה with the scribe's writing and one witness
steps.stepSummary: A story: רבי אבהו wanted to accept a כתובה backed by the scribe's known handwriting and one known signature.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain marriage contract came before רבי אבהו. People recognized its text and the signature of one witness. He thought to declare it valid.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story that tests the rule from the משנה. This sets up רבי ירמיה's reaction in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Only two things could be confirmed: the handwriting of the text, which was the scribe's, and one witness's signature. רבי אבהו read the משנה as 'the scribe wrote,' so he thought this counted as two witnesses.

keyTerms.meaning: A marriage contract (literally, a grooms' כתובה)
The written body of the document, in the scribe's handwriting

phrases.english: There was a certain marriage contract
that came before Rabbi Abbahu,
where they recognized its written text,
phrases.notes: Recognizing the text means they knew the scribe's handwriting.

phrases.english: and the handwritten signature of one witness.
He thought to declare it valid,

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהִיא כְּתוּבַּת חֲתָנִים דַּאֲתַאי לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי אֲבָהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the משנה's line to a real case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי אבהו leaned toward accepting a document backed by the scribe's handwriting plus one witness.

steps.title: רבי ירמיה stops רבי אבהו
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה tells רבי אבהו that the משנה says 'the scribe signed,' so handwriting alone doesn't count.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה said to him: We learned 'the scribe signed.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ירמיה pushes back on רבי אבהו's plan. He repeats his reading of the משנה from step 15.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this כתובה, the scribe only wrote the text and never signed it, so there was really only one witness. Since the משנה requires the scribe to have signed, the כתובה cannot be confirmed this way.
steps.whatToRemember: A scribe counts as a witness only by signing. His handwriting in the text plus one witness is not two witnesses.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya said to him:
We learned: 'the scribe signed.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה חָתַם סוֹפֵר שָׁנִינוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רבי אבהו's plan to accept the כתובה.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects accepting the כתובה based on the scribe's handwriting plus one witness.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: רבי אבהו read the משנה as 'the scribe wrote,' but the correct reading is 'the scribe signed.'
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Without the scribe's actual signature, one witness is not enough to confirm the document.

steps.title: The משנה: writing a nickname is valid
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a new line from the משנה: if the scribe wrote the husband's or wife's nickname in the גט, it is valid.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he wrote his nickname and her nickname, the גט is valid.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new line of the משנה, about writing nicknames in a גט. It is setting up the discussion that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a גט names the husband and wife. The משנה teaches that a nickname or family name people know them by is also good enough. The next step asks how far back such a family name may go.

keyTerms.meaning: A nickname or family surname that a person is known by

phrases.english: If he wrote his nickname and her nickname, it is valid.
phrases.notes: This is the next line of the משנה. 'He' is the scribe writing the גט.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: New line of the משנה, unrelated to the scribe-signature discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A גט that uses the husband's or wife's nickname is valid.

steps.title: How many generations an ancestral nickname lasts
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא: the first opinion says a family nickname from ancestors works for ten generations; רבי שמעון בן אלעזר says only three.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: a nickname from the forefathers is valid in a גט for up to ten generations. רבי שמעון בן אלעזר says it is valid for three generations, and after that it is invalid.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא about a family name that comes from an ancestor. Two opinions disagree on how long that name still identifies someone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A family nickname is only useful if people still connect it to this family. The ת"ק thinks it stays recognized for ten generations. רבי שמעון בן אלעזר thinks it fades after three, so after that it no longer identifies the person.

keyTerms.meaning: A family nickname inherited from ancestors

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
A nickname from the forefathers in bills of divorce
is valid up to ten generations.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says:
For three generations it is valid;
from here onward it is invalid.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds detail on how long a family nickname from the משנה stays valid.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ת"ק: ten generations. רבי שמעון בן אלעזר: three generations, then invalid.

steps.title: Whose view is רבי חנינא's three-generation rule?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which opinion matches רבי חנינא's rule that an ancestral nickname works for up to three generations.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whose opinion does רבי חנינא follow when he said that writing a nickname from the forefathers in a גט is valid for up to three generations?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes רבי חנינא and asks which side of the ברייתא he follows. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי חנינא gives a number, three generations, without saying where it comes from. The גמרא wants to tie his rule to one of the two opinions just quoted.

phrases.english: Whose opinion does it follow,
this that Rabbi Chanina said:
If he wrote a nickname from the forefathers in bills of divorce,
it is valid up to three generations?

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּמַאן אָזְלָא הָא דְּאָמַר רַבִּי חֲנִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Connects an אמורא's rule to the ברייתא just quoted.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which תנא in the ברייתא does רבי חנינא's three-generation rule match?

steps.title: It follows רבי שמעון בן אלעזר
steps.stepSummary: The answer: רבי חנינא follows רבי שמעון בן אלעזר.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whose? It follows רבי שמעון בן אלעזר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its own question: רבי חנינא's rule is the view of רבי שמעון בן אלעזר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Only רבי שמעון בן אלעזר used the number three. So רבי חנינא, also saying three, matches him and not the ten-generation view.

phrases.english: Whose? It follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 21.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי חנינא follows רבי שמעון בן אלעזר's three-generation view.

steps.title: רב הונא's source: 'ונושנתם'
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא gives a פסוק behind the three-generation limit: 'children and grandchildren, and you will grow old.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said: What is the source? 'When you have children and grandchildren and you will have grown old.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא brings a פסוק as the source for the three-generation rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק lists children, then grandchildren, and then uses 'ונושנתם', from the word for 'old.' This shows that after about three generations things count as old and forgotten. So an ancestral nickname stops identifying the family after that.

keyTerms.meaning: And you will have grown old

steps.whyThisMatters: It gives a source in the פסוק for רבי שמעון בן אלעזר's view.

phrases.english: Rav Huna said:
What is the verse?
"When you beget children and children's children,
and you will have grown old."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a source for the three-generation view just identified.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'ונושנתם' after children and grandchildren shows that after three generations a matter is old and forgotten.

steps.title: Seven idol-worshipping royal courts before the destruction
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן לוי: ארץ ישראל was not destroyed until seven royal courts worshipped idols. He names them and brings a פסוק in ירמיה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהושע בן לוי said: ארץ ישראל was not destroyed until seven royal courts worshipped idols in it: ירבעם בן נבט, בעשא בן אחיה, אחאב בן עמרי, יהוא בן נמשי, פקח בן רמליהו, מנחם בן גדי, and הושע בן אלה. As it says: 'She who bore seven languishes, her spirit droops, her sun set while it was still day, she is ashamed and disgraced.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to an aggadic teaching about why the land was destroyed. רבי יהושע בן לוי lists seven kings and supports it with a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The punishment did not come right away. It came only after seven kings and their courts had led the people into עבודה זרה. The 'seven' in the פסוק in ירמיה is read as these seven dynasties.

keyTerms.meaning: Courts (here, royal houses and their courts)
As it is said (introduces a פסוק)

steps.whatToRemember: An ancestral nickname works in a גט for three generations according to רבי שמעון בן אלעזר (and רבי חנינא), learned from 'ונושנתם'. The land was destroyed only after seven idol-worshipping royal courts.
steps.confusionAlert: The 'בתי דינים' here are not ordinary courts of judges. They are the royal houses of these kings, together with their courts, who led the people into idol worship.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said:
The Land of Israel was not destroyed
until there worshipped in it
seven royal courts, worshipping idols;
and these are they:
Jeroboam son of Nevat,
and Baasha son of Ahijah,
and Ahab son of Omri,
and Jehu son of Nimshi,
and Pekah son of Remaliah,
and Menahem son of Gadi,
and Hoshea son of Elah.
As it is said:
"She who bore seven languishes,
her spirit droops,
her sun has set while it was still day,
she is ashamed and disgraced."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי לֹא חָרְבָה אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the halacha of nicknames to an aggadic teaching about the destruction of the land.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ארץ ישראל was destroyed only after seven royal courts worshipped idols, as hinted by 'יולדת השבעה'.

steps.title: The verse behind the seven royal courts
steps.stepSummary: רב אמי brings a פסוק as the source for רבי יהושע בן לוי's teaching about seven royal courts.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אמי said: What is the source? The פסוק says, "When you have children and grandchildren."
steps.whatsHappening: רב אמי finds a פסוק that hints at the seven royal courts mentioned in step 24.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק in דברים warns that after generations of children and grandchildren, the people will sin and be removed from the land. The words for 'beget' and 'children' are read as counting generations, and the total comes to seven. The idea is that the exile came only after seven generations of kings, as the פסוק hinted.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the verse? (asking for the source in the תורה)

steps.confusionAlert: In step 23, רב הונא used words from this same פסוק to teach a three-generation limit. Here רב אמי uses it for a different teaching, the seven royal courts.

phrases.english: Rav Ami said:
What is the verse?
"When you will have children and grandchildren."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a source in the תורה for רבי יהושע בן לוי's count of seven royal courts.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The seven royal courts before the destruction are hinted at in the פסוק 'כי תוליד בנים ובני בנים'.

steps.title: Why was the exile in the days of a less wicked king?
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא and רב אסי point out that הושע בן אלה was better than the kings before him, yet the Assyrian exile came in his time.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא and רב אסי said to רב: The פסוק says that הושע בן אלה did evil, but not like the kings of ישראל before him. Yet the next פסוק says that שלמנאסר came up against him. Why?
steps.whatsHappening: Two students ask רב a hard question. Why did the punishment fall on a king who was less wicked than the ones before him?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק itself says that הושע was better than the earlier kings. Even so, the exile by שלמנאסר happened in his days. This does not seem fair, so they ask what was different about his generation.

keyTerms.meaning: the last king of the northern kingdom of ישראל
king of Assyria who attacked and exiled ישראל

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ רַב כָּהֲנָא וְרַב אַסִּי לְרַב,
phrases.english: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi said to Rav:
It is written about Hoshea ben Elah:
"And he did evil in the eyes of God,
only not like the kings of Israel"
and it is written: "Against him came up Shalmaneser, etc."?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ רַב כָּהֲנָא וְרַב אַסִּי לְרַב, כְּתִיב בֵּיהּ בְּהוֹשֵׁעַ בֶּן אֵלָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the timing of the exile that ended the line of sinful kings described in step 24.
steps.kashyaTarget: The fact that the exile came in the days of הושע בן אלה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Two פסוקים seem to clash: הושע was less wicked than earlier kings, yet he received the harshest punishment.

steps.title: The people did not go up for the festival
steps.stepSummary: רב answers that הושע removed ירבעם's guards, but the people still did not go up to ירושלים, so the exile came then.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said to them: ירבעם had set guards on the roads to stop ישראל from going up for the רגל. הושע came and removed them. Even so, the people did not go up. God said: For those years they did not go up for the רגל, they will go into captivity.
steps.whatsHappening: רב answers the question. Once the king was no longer stopping them, the people had no excuse, so the blame was now on them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under earlier kings, the people could say the king's guards stopped them. הושע took away that excuse, but they still stayed home. So the sin became the people's own, and the people were punished with exile.

keyTerms.meaning: guards or checkpoints on the roads
the first king of the northern kingdom
going up to ירושלים for the festival pilgrimage

steps.whatToRemember: The exile came in הושע's days because the people chose not to go up for the רגל even when nothing stopped them. Their excuse was gone.

phrases.english: He said to them:

phrases.aramaic: אוֹתָן פַּרְדְּסִיאוֹת שֶׁהוֹשִׁיב יָרׇבְעָם עַל הַדְּרָכִים
phrases.english: Those guards that Jeroboam placed on the roads
so that Israel would not go up for the festival,
Hoshea came and removed them,

phrases.aramaic: וְאַף עַל פִּי כֵן לֹא עָלוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל לָרֶגֶל.
phrases.english: and even so, Israel did not go up for the festival.
The Holy One, Blessed be He, said:

phrases.aramaic: אוֹתָן שָׁנִים שֶׁלֹּא עָלוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל לָרֶגֶל –
phrases.english: For those years that Israel did not go up for the festival,
they will go into captivity.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהוּ: אוֹתָן פַּרְדְּסִיאוֹת שֶׁהוֹשִׁיב יָרׇבְעָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of רב כהנא and רב אסי.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains a hidden factor: the people's own sin in הושע's time
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The punishment should follow the king's level of wickedness, so הושע's generation should have been spared.
steps.terutzMaskana: Once הושע removed the obstacle and the people still did not go up for the רגל, the guilt was theirs, and the exile came.

steps.title: How can God's righteousness bring disaster?
steps.stepSummary: מרימר opens a teaching on a פסוק in דניאל. He asks how the פסוק can link God being צדיק with Him bringing evil upon ישראל.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said in the name of מר עוקבא (some say רב חסדא said in the name of רבי ירמיה): מרימר taught: What does the פסוק mean, "God watched over the evil and brought it upon us, for the Lord our God is righteous"? Because God is righteous, He watched over the evil and brought it on us?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a new teaching. מרימר raises a puzzle in a פסוק, and the answer comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק seems to say that God brought disaster because He is righteous. That sounds strange, because righteousness should lead to kindness, not punishment. מרימר's question prepares us for a surprising explanation.

keyTerms.meaning: and some say (a different chain of names)
taught a פסוק by explaining it in depth
and He watched over (was careful about the timing of)

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר מָר עוּקְבָא,
phrases.english: Rav Chisda said that Mar Ukva said,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי לַהּ אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה,
phrases.english: and some say Rav Chisda said that Rabbi Yirmeya said,
Mareimar taught:
What is the meaning of what is written:
"And God watched over the evil and brought it upon us,
for the Lord our God is righteous"?
Because "the Lord our God is righteous,"
"God watched over the evil and brought it upon us"?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new teaching about the destruction and exile, after the discussion of הושע בן אלה is finished.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How the פסוק can say that God's righteousness is the reason He brought disaster on ישראל.

steps.title: God was kind by sending the scholars into exile first
steps.stepSummary: The answer to מרימר's question: God did צדקה with ישראל, because when צדקיהו's exile came, the earlier exile of יכניה, which included the great scholars, was still there to guide them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, God did a kindness with ישראל: He brought the exile of צדקיהו while the exile of יכניה was still standing. About the exile of יכניה it is written: 'the craftsmen and the smiths, a thousand.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers מרימר's question. The 'evil' God hurried was actually wrapped in kindness.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The kindness was in the timing. The great scholars had already gone into exile with יכניה years earlier. So when the larger exile of צדקיהו came, the Jewish people found Torah leaders already waiting for them in בבל.

keyTerms.meaning: The later exile, at the time of the חורבן, under King צדקיהו
The earlier exile under King יכניה, which included the great scholars
Literally 'the craftsmen and the smiths'; here read as the Torah scholars

steps.confusionAlert: צדקה here does not mean money given to the poor. It means God acting kindly toward ישראל in the middle of the punishment.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא צְדָקָה עָשָׂה הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
phrases.english: Rather, the Holy One, Blessed be He, did a kindness
with ישראל, in that He brought about the exile of צדקיהו
while the exile of יכניה was still standing,
phrases.notes: The people exiled with יכניה were still alive in בבל, so they were there to help the new arrivals.

phrases.english: as it is written about the exile of יכניה:
"The craftsmen and the smiths, a thousand";
phrases.notes: מלכים ב 24:16. The גמרא reads these as the great Torah scholars, as the next lines explain.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא צְדָקָה עָשָׂה הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא עִם יִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question מרימר raised in step 28
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: God's צדקה was sending the scholars ahead with יכניה, so they could guide the people exiled with צדקיהו.

steps.title: Why the scholars are called 'חרש' and 'מסגר'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains the two nicknames: חרש, because everyone was like deaf people when the scholars spoke; מסגר, because once they closed a question, no one could reopen it. There were a thousand of them.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'חרש': when they opened a Torah topic, everyone became like deaf people. 'מסגר': once they closed a topic, no one opened it again. And how many were there? A thousand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pauses to explain the words of the פסוק it just quoted. It shows why these words describe great scholars.
steps.deeperAnalysis: חרש sounds like חֵרֵשׁ, a deaf person: the scholars' Torah was so deep that the listeners could not follow it. מסגר comes from 'closing': a question these scholars could not settle, no one else could ever settle. This shows how great the scholars sent ahead were.

keyTerms.meaning: They open, meaning they start a Torah discussion
They close, meaning they shut a discussion they could not settle

phrases.english: "חרש": because when they would open a topic,
everyone became like deaf people.
phrases.notes: It's a wordplay: חרש is spelled like חֵרֵשׁ, deaf. The listeners couldn't follow, as if they couldn't hear.

phrases.english: "מסגר": once they closed a topic,
no one would open it again.
And how many were they? A thousand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the words of the פסוק quoted in step 29
steps.mimraCoreRuling: חרש and מסגר describe a thousand outstanding Torah scholars exiled with יכניה.

steps.title: עולא: the exile came two years early
steps.stepSummary: עולא gives a different answer: God's צדקה was that He brought the exile two years earlier than the number hinted in the word 'ונושנתם'.
steps.simpleTranslation: עולא said: God's kindness was that He brought the exile two years before 'ונושנתם'.
steps.whatsHappening: עולא offers a second, separate answer to מרימר's question. For him the kindness is about when the exile came.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק in דברים warns that after 'ונושנתם', a long stay in the land, the people will sin and be utterly destroyed from the land (דברים 4:26). The letters of ונושנתם add up to 852, but God sent the exile after 850 years, so that the threat of total destruction would never come true. That is why bringing the exile early counts as צדקה.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who gives the second answer
'And you will have grown old (in the land)', a word from the תורה's warning about exile

steps.whatToRemember: Two answers explain how God's 'hurrying the evil' was צדקה: sending the scholars ahead with יכניה, or (עולא) bringing the exile two years early.

phrases.english: עולא said:
that He brought it two years earlier than "ונושנתם".
phrases.notes: דברים 4:25. The letters of ונושנתם add up to 852, and the exile came after 850 years in the land.

steps.triggerLanguage: עוּלָּא אָמַר: שֶׁהִקְדִּים שְׁתֵּי שָׁנִים לִוְנוֹשַׁנְתֶּם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second answer to מרימר's question, alongside the answer in step 29
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: God's צדקה was bringing the exile two years before the time hinted in 'ונושנתם'.
